payload.problem_addressed: Verifier-free test-time scaling (VF-TTS) for LLM reasoning breaks down on hard problems: simple confidence-maximization selection favors 'confidently wrong' answers when a model must explore multiple solution paths.
payload.method_summary: Introduces 'consilience', a verifier-free rollout-selection metric that scores each reasoning trace by its confidence trajectory, explicitly penalizing high initial confidence (which signals a failure to explore alternatives) while still rewarding high final confidence (convergence to an answer).
payload.contributions_summary: The paper shows confidence-based verifier-free test-time scaling catastrophically breaks down on hard problems because uniformly high confidence often marks a failure to explore rather than correctness. It introduces consilience, a metric that evaluates the temporal asymmetry of a rollout's confidence trajectory (low-then-high) to pick better completions without any external verifier. Experiments on graduate math, QA, and free-form code generation show consilience beats confidence-maximization and matches or exceeds verifier-based selection in some settings. It notably works in domains like free-form code generation where voting-based selection is inapplicable.
key_architecture_choices: Token-level confidence trajectory tracked across the reasoning phase
Reasoning-phase isolation to separate exploratory vs conclusion segments
Combinatorial score penalizing early confidence while rewarding final confidence
payload.headline_results: On LiveCodeBench, consilience raises GPT-OSS-120B accuracy to 69.7%, substantially outperforming Pass@1 (65.7%); similar gains reported on other reasoning-heavy datasets.
claimed_advantages: Fully verifier-free -- no compiler, test cases, or trained value function required
Near-zero overhead, applicable even where voting-based selection is inapplicable (free-form code)
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Hexgen screens best-of-N candidate programs with an expensive frozen machine-checkable verifier. Consilience's confidence-trajectory signal could serve as a cheap, verifier-free pre-filter or complementary ranking over decoder rollouts -- e.g. to triage which of N sampled programs to run through the verifier first under a compute budget, or as an additional selection signal alongside the verifier's pass/fail result.
payload.reviewer_notes: Validated only on free-form LLM token-level reasoning (math/code/QA); hexgen's decoder emits short DSL programs via pointer/copy heads over a small closed vocabulary, a very different confidence regime, so it's unclear the same low-then-high confidence signature would emerge -- would need empirical validation on hexgen's own rollouts before relying on it to replace/triage the frozen verifier.

provenance.problem_addressed: confidence-based VF-TTS methods... catastrophically break down on complex tasks
provenance.method_summary: a novel selection framework that explicitly evaluates the temporal asymmetry of confidence in reasoning
provenance.headline_results: elevates the GPT-OSS-120B model to an accuracy of 69.7%, substantially outperforming Pass@1 (65.7%)
provenance.claimed_advantages: introduce near-zero overhead for sample evaluation and require minimal access to internal model states

payload.problem_addressed: Selecting the best candidate among multiple LLM-sampled text-to-CAD programs at test time, when no ground truth is available and a separate verifier/judge is undesirable or unavailable.
payload.method_summary: 3D CAD consensus selection: sample N parametric CAD programs from an LLM, compile each to a 3D model, and return the candidate whose compiled geometry or topology agrees most with the rest of the pool, using either a geometric agreement metric or a topological agreement metric.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper proposes verifier-free 'consensus selection' for text-to-CAD generation: instead of using a separate vision-language judge, it compiles every sampled candidate program to a 3D model and picks the one that agrees most with the rest of the pool, under geometric or topological notions of agreement. On the candidate pools of a state-of-the-art CAD generation method, geometric consensus improves all three geometric metrics over that method's own verifier, and topological consensus matches it on topology. The method is training-free and works across every tested LLM and prompt variant, reducing Chamfer distance by 1-10% versus random selection from the same pool.
key_architecture_choices: Training-free, verifier-free candidate selection (no external judge model)
Geometric agreement metric comparing compiled 3D geometry across the candidate pool
Topological agreement metric comparing B-rep/topological structure across the candidate pool
payload.headline_results: Geometric consensus improves all three geometric metrics over the base method's own verifier and reduces Chamfer distance by 1-10% versus random selection, across every tested LLM and prompt variant.
claimed_advantages: No external verifier or vision-language judge needed
Training-free and compatible as a drop-in with existing CAD generation agents
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Directly applicable to hexgen's best-of-N candidate screening: alongside (or as a cheap pre-filter before) the frozen machine-checkable verifier, a consensus/agreement score computed across the compiled meshes of the N sampled hex-meshing programs could re-rank or triage candidates using signal the pool itself provides, potentially reducing how often the expensive verifier must run.
payload.reviewer_notes: Consensus selection implicitly assumes the majority of sampled candidates are 'roughly correct', so the informative signal is majority agreement; if hexgen's decoder occasionally produces a correct-but-structurally-distinct minority candidate (e.g. a valid but unusual block/sweep decomposition), consensus selection could systematically penalize good outliers -- worth checking against hexgen's actual candidate-pool diversity before adopting wholesale.
dependencies_on_other_methods: Requires an existing text-to-CAD (or here, B-rep-to-program) generator that produces a candidate pool to select from

provenance.problem_addressed: a single sample is often wrong... yet no ground-truth model is available at generation time
provenance.method_summary: sample N parametric CAD programs, compile them to 3D models, and return the candidate that agrees most with the rest of the pool
provenance.claimed_advantages: The method is training-free and compatible with existing CAD agents

payload.problem_addressed: Existing CAD-generation evaluations judge only whether a model looks correct; they don't test whether generated/edited CAD is engineering-grade -- satisfying design requirements, responding predictably to parameter edits, matching a reference structural response, or connecting to other parts through valid joints.
payload.method_summary: CADEngBench, a two-track benchmark: CADEngBench-P evaluates 300 parametric parts on B-Rep validity, engineering/DFM checks, parameter-family perturbations, functional editing, and matched linear-static FEA (via CalculiX); CADEngBench-A evaluates 150 body pairs on ranked joint retrieval, exact face-and-edge grounding, joint-frame prediction, and kinematic verification.
payload.contributions_summary: The paper argues CAD evaluation must test engineering behavior, not just visual/geometric correctness, and introduces CADEngBench to do so. CADEngBench-P covers 600 zero-to-CAD and functional-editing tasks over 300 parametric parts, checked via B-Rep validity, DFM rules, parameter perturbations, and matched FEA simulation. CADEngBench-A covers 150 assembly body pairs, testing joint retrieval, face/edge grounding, joint-frame prediction, and kinematic verification. Evaluating eight multimodal, code-capable models shows editing supplied CAD is much easier than generating it from scratch, complex edits and matched FEA remain hard, and assembly predictions often find the right region but miss the exact joint or mating entities.
key_architecture_choices: Two-track benchmark design: parametric-part track (CADEngBench-P) and assembly track (CADEngBench-A)
Boundary-representation (B-Rep) validity checking as a core evaluation axis
Matched linear-static FEA in CalculiX to test whether generated/edited parts meet a declared structural response
Parameter-family perturbations to test robustness of generated CAD under parameter changes
payload.headline_results: Across eight multimodal, code-capable models, editing supplied CAD is substantially easier than generating it from scratch; complex edits and matched FEA remain difficult; assembly predictions often locate the relevant region but fail to recover the exact recorded joint or mating entities.
claimed_advantages: Tests engineering-grade correctness (structural response, DFM, valid joints), not just visual/geometric similarity
Covers both single-part generation/editing and multi-body assembly reasoning in one benchmark
payload.applicability_to_our_problem: Directly on-target for hexgen: CADEngBench's B-Rep-validity and matched-FEA-style evaluation methodology is close kin to hexgen's own frozen verifier (compiles, zero inverted elements, scaled-Jacobian/aspect-ratio bounds, surface-match fidelity). Its finding that 'editing is easier than generating' and that complex edits/FEA remain hard is a useful calibration point for how hard the hexgen program-generation task should be expected to be, and its parameter-family-perturbation protocol is a candidate template for stress-testing hexgen's generalization to nearby part variants.
payload.reviewer_notes: This is a benchmark/evaluation paper, not a method paper -- it doesn't propose a generation technique to borrow, but it's a strong candidate source of evaluation methodology (B-Rep validity + FEA-matched checks + parameter perturbations) that hexgen's own verifier design could be compared against or extended with.

provenance.problem_addressed: A CAD model is not engineering-grade merely because it looks correct.
provenance.method_summary: CADEngBench-P evaluates 300 parametric parts... through boundary-representation (B-Rep) validity, engineering and DFM checks, parameter-family perturbations, functional editing, and matched linear-static FEA in CalculiX
provenance.headline_results: editing supplied CAD is substantially easier than generating it, while complex edits and matched FEA remain difficult
provenance.claimed_advantages: These results show that CAD evaluation must test engineering behavior rather than appearance alone

payload.effort_rationale: Requires implementing a geometric/topological agreement metric over compiled hex-mesh outputs; moderate build but reuses existing compile/verify infrastructure.
